title: BEAM updates fire only on a 2.4% utilization deviation after the cooldown has elapsed
content:
A.4.4.1.3.8.6.2.1 defines when the automated process should act: parameters "should be updated if (1) the current Utilization deviates from the Utilization as of the last time the stUSDS parameters were set by more than 2.4% and (2) the time since the last update is greater than `tau`."

Both conditions are necessary, and each rules out a distinct pathology. Without a **deviation threshold**, a controller tracking a continuously varying input would update perpetually, paying gas and generating governance noise for changes users cannot perceive. Without the **time condition**, a period of genuine volatility would produce a burst of rapid updates, making the borrow and supply rates themselves a source of instability for anyone trying to plan around them.

Using deviation *from the last set point* rather than from a target is the detail that makes this a hysteresis band rather than a tolerance. Parameters are allowed to be wrong by up to 2.4% of utilization indefinitely, and the system only re-anchors when reality has moved meaningfully away from where it last committed. That is the standard cure for controller chatter around a threshold.

The cost is accepted staleness: between updates the published rate is knowingly off the formula's ideal, and in a fast crunch the parameters lag by up to `tau`. Since `tau` is also the module's hard cooldown, the trigger cannot be satisfied more often than the envelope permits — the update rule and the security bound are deliberately the same clock.
description: A two-condition trigger — magnitude plus elapsed tau — creates deliberate hysteresis, so parameters track real shifts instead of chasing noise or burning gas on trivial adjustments.
